items.title: A Big Online Store Got Hacked — Change That Password
items.summary: A hacker broke into ASOS, the big online clothing store, and walked off with customer information. The company confirmed the break-in this week after shoppers started seeing strange messages. If you have an ASOS account, change that password today — and never reuse it anywhere else. Crooks who steal one password try it on your email and your bank next. I've had customers lose an account for exactly this reason. Two minutes now saves a world of grief.

items.title: Need to split or combine a PDF? Firefox's free built-in PDF editor does it at firefox.com — no Adobe needed
items.summary: Update Firefox free at firefox.com (or click Menu → Help → About to get the newest version). Open any PDF in Firefox, click the little page-thumbnail icon in the top-left corner, and you get a toolbar that can split, merge, reorder, rotate, and add pages. Then save it. You never upload the file to a website and you never pay a subscription — it all happens on your own computer.

items.title: Stop reusing one password everywhere — Proton Pass is the free password manager that fills in your logins, at proton.me/pass
items.summary: Go to proton.me/pass and create a free account. Proton Pass remembers every password, makes up strong new ones for you, and fills them in automatically on your computer. The free plan has no limit on how many passwords you can store, and you only have to remember the one that unlocks the app.

items.title: That 'I'm Not a Robot' Box Is a Trick
items.summary: Fake "I'm not a robot" boxes are showing up in search results and on random websites. They look harmless, but they tell you to press a few keys and paste something into a little box to prove you're a person. Do that and you've just started a bad program on your computer. Real checks never ask you to press keys or paste anything — so close the tab. I've had two machines come in this month with exactly this. According to a new report, most now arrive straight from search results.

items.title: Microsoft is turning on a free Windows safety feature called Core isolation this month — check yours at Windows Security > Device security
items.summary: Click Start, type Windows Security, and open it. Choose Device security, then click Core isolation details and look at the switch under Core isolation. Microsoft started switching this protection on automatically this month, through the ordinary Windows updates your computer already gets — but not every computer qualifies. If yours is off, turn it on and restart. It is built into Windows, it is free, and there is nothing to buy.

items.title: Computer prices are way up this year because of AI — before you buy anything new, run the free Crucial System Scanner at crucial.com
items.summary: Open your browser and go to crucial.com. Click the System Scanner link, download the free tool, and run it. In about two minutes it reads your exact make and model, shows what parts you already have, and tells you the most your computer can hold. No account, no cost, nothing to sign up for. That way you know what you own before you walk into a store or hand over a credit card.

items.title: A Code You Didn't Ask For — Don't Type It In
items.summary: There's a new way crooks get into your computer and your online accounts without ever learning your password. You get a message with a short code and a link to a real-looking Microsoft or Google page, telling you to type the code in to "confirm" or "protect" your account. Do that, and you've just let them in. My rule is simple: never type a code you didn't ask for. Got one? Delete the message — that's the whole fix.

items.title: Read any web page without the clutter — Microsoft Edge's free Reading mode strips the ads and reads it aloud, just press F9
items.summary: Open the article in Microsoft Edge and press F9, or click the little open-book icon at the right end of the address bar. Edge calls it Reading mode — it hides the ads, the pop-ups, and the "you might also like" clutter, leaving just the words in a bigger, cleaner type. If you'd rather listen, click Read aloud on the small toolbar that appears and the computer reads the whole page to you. It is built into Edge, it is free, and there is nothing to download.

items.title: Type a few words and get a picture — Microsoft Designer's free AI Image Creator makes birthday cards and posters at designer.microsoft.com
items.summary: In any browser go to designer.microsoft.com, sign in with a free Microsoft account (the same one you use for email, if you have it), and type what you want to see — "a birthday card for my granddaughter who loves horses," or "a flyer for our church fish fry on Saturday." Click Create and a few seconds later you'll have finished-looking pictures you can download, print, or share. It is free to use, and you don't need to know anything about art or computers.

items.title: Fake FBI Agents Are Calling — Hang Up and Check
items.summary: Crooks are making fake calls, saying they are FBI, DEA, or Secret Service agents. They make a real agency's phone number show up on your screen and use a real agent's name, then push you to move your money to keep it "safe." The FBI says never send money to anyone claiming to be a federal agent. If this happens to you, it's a scam — hang up and call the agency yourself at a number you look up. I've had two customers ask me about calls like this just this week.

items.title: Sound and look better on video calls — a Logitech webcam with a built-in microphone is about 40 dollars at logitech.com or Amazon
items.summary: Buy a Logitech webcam — the C270 is about 40 dollars and the C920 is about 60 — from logitech.com, Amazon, or Walmart. Plug the USB cable into your computer and you're done; there's nothing to install on Windows or a Mac. You get a much sharper picture and a microphone that doesn't echo, so family, doctors, and work calls can actually see and hear you.

items.title: Type and click without touching the keyboard — Windows Voice Access is built into Windows 11, free at Settings > Accessibility > Speech
items.summary: Open Settings > Accessibility > Speech and turn on Voice access. Then just talk: say "open my email," "click Save," or "type Dear Mary" and Windows does it for you. It's built into Windows 11, costs nothing, needs no account, and works even without internet. If your hands ache, your keyboard is acting up, or you'd simply rather talk than type, this turns your computer into a hands-free machine.
